observations:
Torah #84 is a short, structurally tight teaching (11 lines) built around a single Talmudic question-and-answer (Megillah 28: 'With what did you lengthen your days? — I was generous with my money'). The teaching draws its conceptual architecture entirely from a Zohar passage (Parshat Nasso p. 123) and a Tikkunei Zohar citation (Tikkun 70), and all bechina equivalences are clustered into three well-defined packages already proposed:

  Package 1 — מִדַּת אַבְרָהָם וְסִטְרָא דִּימִינָא (good) — 5 nodes, 4 bechina edges
  Package 2 — מַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת וּמְקַטְרְגִים (evil) — 3 nodes, 2 bechina edges
  Package 3 — הַטּוֹב הַגָּנוּז וְרָזִין דְּאוֹרַיְתָא (good) — 2 nodes, 1 bechina edge

The criteria for a NEW package (as opposed to adding missing nodes to existing packages) are: three or more concepts with bechina language forming an INDEPENDENT conceptual domain not covered by the three packages above.

Analysis of remaining source-text concepts not yet in a package:

1. שֵׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְּרֵאשִׁית (six days of creation): mentioned as the structural backdrop (each day has a partzuf and a hidden good), but connected to the other concepts only by eitza (the hidden good belongs to each day; accessing the gate leads into that day's good). No bechina language links it to other nodes as sharing the same essential nature.

2. חֹשֶׁךְ (darkness as barrier): described functionally as the 'gadder' (outer fence) hiding the light/good of each day. Its nature is implicit — it is the obstructing force around the day's good — but it is not equated via 'הַיְנוּ' or 'הוּא בחינת' to any other concept in this Torah specifically. It could reasonably be associated with Package 2's blocking forces (functionally identical), but the text does not supply an explicit bechina equation. Without explicit bechina language, this node cannot be added to the dataset as a bechina edge.

3. קָטֵגוֹר נַעֲשֶׂה סַנֵּגוֹר (accuser becomes defender): this is explicitly a transformation (eitza), not a parallel-nature statement. The Zohar says the accusers 'become' defenders for the righteous person — this is a directional, causal change, not a statement that accusers and defenders share the same essential nature.

4. תַּרְעָא דִּתְשׁוּבָה (gate of repentance): mentioned in the Zohar as an alternative entry gate. While it is structurally parallel to תַּרְעָא דְּאַהֲבָה (both are gates through which one enters the hidden good), the Torah does not supply any bechina equation connecting it to a specific person, trait, or side of the sefirot. In other Torahs of Likutay Moharan, teshuvah is associated with the left side and with Isaac/gevurah — but that connection is not made here in Torah 84. Adding it here without explicit textual support would introduce cross-Torah inference rather than Torah-84-specific bechina data.

5. הַיָּמִים הַגְּדוֹלִים / הַאֲרָכַת יָמִים (long/great days): these appear as the eitza-outcome of using Abraham's quality — they are what results from entering the hidden good of each day. Not equated via bechina to other concepts within this Torah.

Conclusion: The three packages above cover all bechina-connected concepts in Torah 84. No additional independent conceptual domain of three or more bechina-linked nodes exists in the source text that would justify a new package. The remaining source-text concepts are either connected only by eitza, are implicit/functional rather than explicit bechina equivalences, or would require cross-Torah inference to package. Torah #84 is complete with 3 packages, 10 nodes, and 7 bechina edges.
